Pharmacokinetics: what the body does to a drug
Leonard, Fundamentals of Psychopharmacology, Chapter 3

Same pill, same dose, three different stories

Rx Escitalopram 10 mg, once a day, for depression

Ayesha

“After a few weeks I feel like myself again.”

No other medicines.

Bilal

“Nausea, dizziness. It feels far too strong.”

Also buys omeprazole at the pharmacy for acidity.

Sana

“Two months on it. Nothing has changed.”

Also takes carbamazepine for epilepsy.

Same drug, same dose, same receptors. So why such different results?

Chapter 3 · Introduction · p. 79 Links to Lectures 1–2

Two questions about every drug

Last week · pharmacodynamics

What does the drug do to the body?

Which receptor, transporter or enzyme it acts on, and what changes (blocking reuptake, opening the GABA-A channel…).

Today · pharmacokinetics

What does the body do to the drug?

How much gets in, where it goes, how it is broken down, and how fast it leaves. Together these decide how much drug is at the receptor, and for how long.

A

Absorption
getting into the blood

D

Distribution
spreading around the body

M

Metabolism
chemically changed (Leonard: biotransformation)

E

Excretion
leaving the body

Why it matters: a perfect drug at the receptor is useless if it never gets there, and dangerous if too much of it does.

Absorption · distribution · metabolism · excretion Not in the book: background

Follow one tablet through the body

Start

A tablet is swallowed

It holds millions of drug molecules. Each dot will stand for a crowd of them.

Press → to follow it.

Absorption

1 · Dissolve

The tablet breaks up in the stomach. The drug must dissolve before it can cross into the blood.

Absorption

2 · Cross the gut wall

Fat-soluble molecules slip through the gut lining into tiny veins. These all drain into one vein that goes straight to the liver (the portal vein).

First pass

3 · The liver gets the first bite

Before the drug reaches the rest of the body, the liver breaks down part of it. For the tricyclic antidepressants, about half is lost here.

Distribution

4 · Into the bloodstream

What survives enters the general circulation. The heart pumps it everywhere within about a minute.

Distribution

5 · Brain, fat, everywhere

Fat-soluble drugs cross the blood–brain barrier (Lectures 1–2) and also soak into body fat.

Metabolism

6 · Back to the liver

Each time blood passes through the liver, enzymes change more molecules into water-soluble forms.

Excretion

7 · Out through the kidneys

Water-soluble products are filtered by the kidneys into urine. Some leave in bile or breath.

Afirst passDME

Each dot = a crowd of molecules. Dots that fade at the liver were destroyed before reaching the body.

Chapter 3 · Introduction; first-pass metabolism · pp. 79, 82, 90–91

Which way in? Routes, and who meets the liver first

Bioavailability = the share of a dose that reaches the general blood circulation unchanged.

Injected into a vein: 100% by definition. Swallowed: always less.

Click a route to see the path it takes.

Swallowed

1 down the oesophagus → 2 stomach → 3 small intestine → 4 portal vein to the liver first → 5 heart → 6 brain.

Slowest and the most variable. Lost on the way: drug that never dissolves, drug broken down in the gut wall and liver. Tricyclics lose about 50% to the first pass.

Under the tongue

Mouth lining → veins → heart. Skips the liver.

Example: buprenorphine tablets for opioid dependence dissolve under the tongue.

Into a vein

Straight into the blood. Fastest; bioavailability 100%.

Used in emergencies (e.g. a benzodiazepine for a prolonged seizure). No way to take it back once given.

Into a muscle (depot)

A slowly dissolving store in the muscle leaks into the blood for weeks.

Long-acting antipsychotic injections help people who find daily tablets hard to keep up.

Nasal spray

Lining of the nose → blood. Skips the liver; fast.

Esketamine nasal spray for treatment-resistant depression (approved in the US in 2019).

Skin patch

Slow, steady leak through the skin into the blood for a day or more.

Example: nicotine patches. No first pass, few peaks and troughs.

Chapter 3 · Introduction; first-pass metabolism · pp. 79, 82, 90–91

Bioavailability: how much survives the trip?

Bioavailability = the fraction of a dose that reaches the general circulation unchanged.

Press → to follow 100 molecules.

1 · Not absorbed

Some never dissolve or never cross the gut lining, and leave in the faeces.

2 · Gut wall

Enzymes in the gut lining break some down (this is where grapefruit acts).

3 · Liver, first pass

Everything absorbed from the gut goes to the liver first (portal vein). It changes some molecules. Metabolites still reach the blood, but they don't count: the definition says unchanged.

So, by mouth: always less than 100%

Two reasons: incomplete absorption and breakdown before the general circulation (gut wall + liver). Into a vein skips them all: 100%.

Tricyclics lose about half to the first pass (Leonard).

Chapter 1 recap + Chapter 3 · pp. 79, 86 Lectures 1–2 · the barrier

Remember the gatekeeper? Same rule, whole journey

Last week: the blood–brain barrier

fat-soluble: crosses   charged/water-soluble: turned away

This week: the same rule, everywhere

A fat-soluble drug crosses every fatty membrane, not just the brain's:

  • the gut wall (it is absorbed),
  • into body fat, the placenta and breast milk (it spreads widely),
  • and back out of the kidney tubules, so the body must change it into a water-soluble form before it can leave.

Callbacks: L-DOPA crosses but dopamine can't; carbidopa is designed not to cross (“The L-DOPA trick”). Physostigmine reaches the brain, neostigmine doesn't (“Will it cross?”).

Chapter 3 · Introduction · pp. 79–80

One curve explains onset, strength and duration

Dose

Stomach

Peak: how high, and how soon. Faster absorption → earlier, higher peak.

Window: the effect lasts as long as the level stays above the minimum effective level; it is stronger the further above it the level goes.

Area under the curve: the total amount of drug the body was exposed to.

Dashed: the same dose into a vein (100% reaches the blood). Bioavailability = oral area ÷ vein area. Here 60%: 40% was lost before it reached the general circulation.

CASE REOPENED

Chapter 3 · Introduction · pp. 79–80, 84

How the detective was fooled: volume of distribution

Beaker A · 1 litre of water

+100 mg dye

measured: –100 mg/L

Beaker B · 1 litre + fat

+100 mg dye

measured: –10 mg/L

Vd = amount given ÷ concentration measured

“How much water would I need to dissolve this dose and get this reading?”

A: 100 mg ÷ 100 mg/L = 1 L ✓ the real volume

B: 100 mg ÷ 10 mg/L = 10 L ✗ but there is only 1 L of water!

The fat soaked up 90% of the dye, so the water looks like 10 L. That is an apparent volume.

≈ 8 LWarfarin · stays in the blood (protein-bound)
≈ 30 LAlcohol · spreads through body water
≈ 15 000 LChloroquine · hides in tissues

Why it matters: big Vd = little drug left in the blood for the liver and kidneys to clear, so it lingers (longer half-life), and dialysis can't wash it out (tricyclic overdose).

Chapter 3 · Anxiolytics; drug–protein interactions · pp. 86, 99

Free drug acts; bound drug waits

In the blood, most molecules of many drugs ride on carrier proteins such as albumin, like passengers on a bus.

Press → for two real drugs.

Diazepam · about 2% free

Almost every molecule is on board. Only the free ones can leave the blood, reach the receptor, or be cleared.

Alprazolam · about 30% free

Far more free drug at the same total level.

The bound drug is a reservoir: as free drug is used up, more gets off the bus.

Leonard (p. 99): drug–protein binding interactions seem to matter little in practice for the SSRIs.

Chapter 3 · Introduction · p. 80

Clearance: how fast the filters clean the blood

drug removed per hour = clearance × blood level

Think of a home water filter that cleans 10 litres an hour. The liver and kidneys are the body's filters.

Clearance = 10 L per hour

The volume of blood the body cleans completely of the drug each hour. It is a rate of cleaning, not an amount of drug.

Dirty water: 5 mg/L

10 L/h × 5 mg/L = 50 mg removed per hour.

Cleaner water: 1 mg/L

Same filter: 10 L/h × 1 mg/L = 10 mg per hour. Less drug left, so less removed each hour. That is why the level halves at a steady pace instead of dropping by a fixed amount.

Two filters add up

Total clearance = liver + kidneys (+ small extras: bile, breath). After the break: what makes each filter slow down.

Chapter 3 · Introduction; first-pass metabolism · pp. 79–81, 91, 94

Designing a dose: four numbers, four jobs

Bioavailability

How much of the tablet gets in?

oral dose = injected dose ÷ bioavailability

Drug X: 50% → swallow twice what you would inject.

Volume of distribution

How big is the bath to fill?

loading dose = Vd × target level ÷ bioavailability

100 L × 0.2 mg/L ÷ 0.5 = 40 mg to reach the target at once.

Clearance

How fast does it drain?

dose per hour = clearance × target level ÷ bioavailability

10 L/h × 0.2 mg/L ÷ 0.5 = 4 mg/h ≈ 100 mg a day to keep it there.

Half-life

How often, and how long to settle?

t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ clearance

≈ 7 h → split the dose through the day; steady after ≈ 1½ days (4–5 t½); gone ≈ 1½ days after stopping.

Drug X (made-up, round numbers)

Bioavailability 50% · Vd 100 L · clearance 10 L/h · target level 0.2 mg/L

Routeby mouth, so double
Day 140 mg loading dose (optional)
Then≈ 100 mg a day
How often≈ 33 mg three times a day

And if the patient changes?

Liver disease halves clearance: same dose → level doubles and half-life doubles. Halve the daily dose; it takes twice as long to settle.

2 · A drug is 98% bound to blood proteins. How much of it can act?

Chapter 3 · TCAs; biotransformation · pp. 82–84, 90–92 · Tables 3.1, 3.2

Biotransformation: snip, handle, tag

The problem

Biotransformation (= drug metabolism): the body chemically changes a drug, mostly in the liver.

Amitriptyline loves fat. The kidney filters it, but it slips straight back through the tubule walls into the blood. To leave, it must become water-loving.

Phase 1 · trick 1

Desmethylation: snip off a CH₃

Liver enzymes cut one small carbon group off the nitrogen. Amitriptyline becomes nortriptyline: a smaller molecule, but still the right shape for its target.

Still ACTIVE: a drug in its own right

Phase 1 · trick 2

Hydroxylation: add an –OH handle

CYP2D6 adds an oxygen-hydrogen “handle”. The shape is spoiled and the molecule now likes water a little.

Mostly switched OFF (Leonard: inactive)

Phase 2

Conjugation: bolt a big tag on the handle

A large sugar-acid tag (glucuronic acid) is joined to the –OH. Other tags: acetyl (clonazepam's breakdown product; some MAOIs), sulphate.

OFF and very water-soluble

Shortcut: lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam already have a handle, so they skip phase 1 and go straight to the tag.

Out through the kidney

The purpose of biotransformation: make the drug water-soluble enough to leave in the urine. The rule: a snip often leaves the drug working; a handle or a tag usually switches it off.

Chapter 3 · Antidepressants, anxiolytics, biotransformation · pp. 82–83, 87, 90

Sometimes the “waste product” is a drug too

Diazepam

↓ phase 1

desmethyldiazepam

↓

oxazepam, temazepam

All active. After weeks of use the long-lived metabolite builds up in the brain and does much of the work.

Amitriptyline

↓ phase 1

nortriptyline

Imipramine → desipramine. The “children” block noradrenaline reuptake more, the parents serotonin more, and they last about twice as long.

Fluoxetine

↓ phase 1

norfluoxetine

Active, very long-lasting, and it blocks liver enzymes that other drugs need (slide 21).

Codeine

↓ CYP2D6

morphine

A prodrug: almost all of its pain relief comes from the morphine the liver makes (more in Week 5, on genes).

So: a drug's effect = the parent + its active “children”. The children often have longer half-lives, so effects can outlast the parent drug.

Chapter 3 · Classification of the cytochrome P450 enzymes · pp. 88–93 · Tables 3.1, 3.3 Numbers updated

Meet the liver's workhorses: the CYP450 enzymes

CYP2D6

“Cytochrome P450”: a pigment that absorbs light at 450 nm. Over 80% of prescribed drugs are handled by these enzymes.

2 = the family (at least 40% alike).

D = the subfamily (at least 55% alike).

6 = the individual gene, which makes one enzyme.

1A2

clozapine, olanzapine, tricyclics, caffeine

Sped up by tobacco smoke

2C19

citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline, diazepam, amitriptyline

Its gene varies a lot between people: Week 5

2D6

most tricyclics, paroxetine, fluoxetine, haloperidol, codeine

Blocked by fluoxetine, paroxetine

3A4

alprazolam, midazolam, quetiapine, carbamazepine

Blocked by grapefruit

Why it matters: two drugs that need the same enzyme compete for it. That is the basis of most dangerous drug interactions.

Chapter 3 · Biotransformation; drug–drug interactions · pp. 91–92, 93–95

Jam the machine, or build more machines

Clozapine is cleared mainly by CYP1A2. This patient smokes and is stable on his dose.

Inducer: chemicals in tobacco smoke made his liver build extra CYP1A2. That is why smokers need higher doses.

He stops smoking (or is admitted to a smoke-free ward): the extra enzyme fades within days and his level can rise by up to 50%.

Inhibitor instead: fluvoxamine (an SSRI) jams CYP1A2. In one study clozapine levels rose about 2.3-fold.

Rule of thumb (Leonard): a pharmacokinetic interaction has the same result as changing the dose, even though the prescription never changed.

Chapter 3 · Biotransformation; drug–drug interactions · pp. 91–95 Updated

Interactions hiding in everyday life

A glass of juice

Why do some drug leaflets warn about grapefruit?

Guess firstPhoto: Jedesto, CC BY-SA 4.0

Blocks CYP3A4

Chemicals in grapefruit permanently disable the enzyme in the gut wall, so more drug gets in. One glass can act for up to 3 days.

Discovered by accident (Bailey, 1989).

A cigarette

Does it matter if a patient on clozapine smokes?

Guess firstPhoto: C. E. Vipin, CC BY-SA 2.0

Induces CYP1A2

Tar chemicals (not nicotine) speed up clozapine and olanzapine breakdown. Quitting can push levels up by half.

Prozac + an old antidepressant

A low dose of a tricyclic is added to fluoxetine. Safe?

Guess first

2–3× the tricyclic

Fluoxetine blocks CYP2D6/3A4. Tricyclic levels can rise 2–3-fold: risk of heart rhythm problems.

Two anti-epileptics

Carbamazepine is added to valproate.

Guess first

Toxic by-product

Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4: more valproate becomes a liver-toxic metabolite (“4-ene”).

Chapter 3 · Drug–drug interactions · pp. 93–95

Activity: a “level” or an “action” problem?

Pharmacokinetic

One drug changes how much of the other reaches its target (absorption, breakdown, excretion).

Pharmacodynamic

Both drugs act on the same system, adding to or cancelling each other, even at normal levels.

Click each to sort: first click = kinetic, second = dynamic.

Writing it up: ① define both → ② name the mechanism (enzyme blocked or induced vs same receptor) → ③ one example each, saying what happens to the level: fluvoxamine blocks CYP1A2 → clozapine level rises; alcohol + benzodiazepine both boost GABA-A → level unchanged, sedation adds up.

Chapter 3 · Introduction; lithium · pp. 80, 95–96

Two cleaners: the liver and the kidneys

Liver: changes the drug

  • 🚚 Delivery: how much blood flows through it. Less flow, less cleared.
  • 🔧 Workers: how many enzymes are working. Fewer or blocked enzymes, less cleared.
  • Most psychiatric drugs depend almost entirely on the liver, so small changes in flow or enzymes have big effects.

Kidneys: filter it out

  • Filter the free drug out of the blood into the urine.
  • Water-soluble drugs leave; fat-soluble ones slip back (that is why the liver changes them first).
  • Less water or less kidney blood flow, less cleared.

Who does the cleaning? (approximate share of total clearance)

Escitalopram, most antidepressants and antipsychoticsliver
Pregabalin (anxiety)kidneys: leaves unchanged
Lithiumkidneys only: never metabolised

Chapter 3 · Introduction · p. 80

When the cleaner is overwhelmed: saturation

A shop with one cashier. The cashier is the enzyme; customers are drug molecules.

Quiet shop

Twice the customers, twice the number served per hour. Removal keeps pace with the level: the same fraction goes each hour, so the level halves at a steady rate. This is most drugs at normal doses.

Crowded shop

The cashier is already flat out. More customers just make a longer queue: a fixed amount is removed per hour, however high the level. The half-life gets longer as the level rises.

Why it matters

Phenytoin: a small dose increase can push the level up far more than expected. Overdose: enzymes are swamped, so the poison lingers (tricyclics). Alcohol: the liver clears roughly one drink an hour, however many were drunk.

Chapter 3 · Introduction; biotransformation; TCAs · pp. 80, 84, 92, 99 Updated

What narrows the plughole?

👵

Older age

What changes?

Slower on both cleaners

Less liver blood flow and enzyme work; kidneys filter less each decade. More body fat: a bigger “bath” for fat-soluble drugs. Start low, go slow.

Liver disease

What changes?

Fewer workers

Fewer working enzymes and poorer blood flow. Choose drugs that only need a tag: lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam.

Kidney disease or dehydration

What changes?

Filter clogged

Lithium and pregabalin build up; so can the water-soluble products the liver made. Heat and vomiting count too.

Heart failure

What changes?

Fewer deliveries

A weak pump sends less blood through the liver and kidneys, so both clear less.

👶

Newborn babies

What changes?

Workers still in training

Liver enzymes and kidneys are immature: drugs crossing the placenta or in breast milk linger.

💊

Another medicine

What changes?

Narrower or wider

Inhibitors (fluvoxamine, omeprazole) narrow the plughole; inducers (smoking, carbamazepine) widen it.

Chapter 3 · Plasma neuroleptic concentrations and response · pp. 81–82, 99–100 Updated: brain imaging

Does a blood level tell us if the drug will work?

Leonard, 2003: “controversy still rages”

For antipsychotics, blood levels rarely explained more than 25% of the difference in response. A “therapeutic window” was suspected but unproven.

His hope: brain imaging might one day measure the drug where it acts.

It did: PET scans of D2 receptors

Haloperidol in first-episode psychosis: the share of D2 receptors the drug occupies predicted both benefit and side effects.

Kapur et al. (2000), Am J Psychiatry: 22 patients.

Too little: response unlikely.

The sweet spot: likely to work.

Works, but prolactin rises.

Movement side effects appear.

Chapter 3 · Antidepressants (lithium) · pp. 83–84 Updated: NICE monitoring

Lithium: where blood levels save lives

Target: 0.6–0.8 mmol/L

Blood taken 12 hours after the last dose; checked every 3 months once stable (NICE). The window is narrow: above it lies toxicity.

Press → to see why lithium is so sensitive.

Lithium isn't metabolised at all. The kidney handles it as if it were sodium.

Dehydration (hot weather, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever): the kidney holds on to sodium, and holds on to lithium with it. Levels climb.

Common drugs do the same: ibuprofen and other NSAIDs, “water tablets” (thiazides), some blood-pressure tablets (ACE inhibitors).

Karachi in June: a patient stable all winter can become toxic in a heatwave without any change of dose.

Chapter 3 · Pharmacokinetic aspects of TCAs · pp. 82–84 Unit corrected

Tricyclics: a long-lasting drug with a cliff edge

Long half-life → once at night

Half-lives 12–20 h on average (amitriptyline about 20 h, protriptyline about 80 h); active metabolites last about twice as long. Even longer in older people.

Slows its own absorption

At higher doses its anticholinergic action slows the gut (“rest and digest” blocked, Lectures 1–2), so the tricyclic and any other tablet are absorbed more slowly.

Narrow window

Response is usually around 50–300 ng/mL; toxicity from about 500 ng/mL. A small step up can be dangerous.

When the liver's pathways saturate, raising the dose for a “non-responder” can push the level suddenly into toxicity.

Chapter 3 · Pharmacokinetic aspects of MAOIs · pp. 84–85 Lectures 1–2 · MAO Updated

MAO inhibitors: why cheese became dangerous

Aged cheese, cured meats and soy products contain tyramine. Normally the enzyme MAO in the gut wall and liver destroys it: a first pass we never notice.

Old MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) bind MAO permanently. Tyramine gets through, releases noradrenaline: a dangerous rise in blood pressure.

Because the block is permanent, the effect lasts until the body builds new enzyme: about 2 weeks after the last tablet, though the drug has long left the blood.

Reversible MAO-A inhibitors (moclobemide): a load of tyramine can push the drug off the enzyme in the gut, so tyramine is still destroyed. Far safer with food.

MAO from Lectures 1–2: it breaks down dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin inside the nerve terminal.

Chapter 3 · Plasma anxiolytic concentrations and response · pp. 86–88

Diazepam: the drug that wears off before it leaves

Very fat-soluble: rushes into the brain within minutes. Fast onset.

Then it moves on into body fat. The brain level drops below the effect line in hours, though the drug is still in the body (half-life of a day or more). Distribution, not clearance, ends the effect.

Take it daily and the fat fills up, and the active metabolite builds up: the level now stays high. Sedation and memory problems accumulate, especially in older people.

Lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam skip phase 1: a single glucuronide tag, no active metabolites, little affected by age or liver disease.

Short half-life drugs must be stopped slowly to avoid withdrawal.

1 · A patient on clozapine stops smoking. What should happen to the dose?
2 · An 80-year-old is given the usual adult dose of a drug cleared by the liver. What do you expect?
3 · Why do MAOI effects last 2 weeks after the last tablet?
4 · A single dose of diazepam wears off in hours, yet its half-life is over a day. Why?
5 · Name one thing that can push a lithium level into toxicity without a dose change.

Chapter 3 · Enantiomers: their importance in psychopharmacology · pp. 95–97 Receptors, Lectures 1–2

Left-handed and right-handed molecules

A carbon atom holding four different groups can be built in two ways that are mirror images, like your left and right hands.

The two forms (enantiomers, labelled R and S) have the same atoms and the same chemistry in a test tube…

…but receptors, transporters and enzymes are “handed” too. Like a glove, a receptor fits one hand much better than the other.

Your nose can tell: R-carvone smells of spearmint, S-carvone of caraway. R-limonene smells of oranges, S-limonene of lemon or pine.

Many psychiatric drugs are sold as a 50:50 mix of both forms: a racemate. Selling just the useful one is a chiral switch.

Chapter 3 · Enantiomers · pp. 96–99 Updated outcomes

Chiral switches: hits and misses

Citalopram → escitalopram

Keep only the S form of an SSRI?

Hit or miss?

Hit · approved 2002

S form is over 100× stronger at blocking serotonin reuptake; the R form may even work against it. Similar or slightly better tolerability.

Bupivacaine → levobupivacaine

A local anaesthetic that stopped hearts.

Hit or miss?

Hit

The heart toxicity sat mainly in the R form; the single S form is a safer anaesthetic.

Fenfluramine → dexfenfluramine

A “purer” appetite suppressant.

Hit or miss?

Miss · withdrawn 1997

More effective, but linked to heart-valve damage and lung (pulmonary) hypertension.

Zopiclone → eszopiclone

Leonard (2003) suggested the R form might avoid hangover.

What happened?

The S form won · US 2004

S-zopiclone carries the binding power (about 50× the R form) and was marketed as eszopiclone.

Thioridazine

An antipsychotic whose forms and metabolites differ in many ways.

What happened?

Too complex · withdrawn 2005

A heart-rhythm (QT) risk led the maker to withdraw it worldwide before any switch was made.

Ketamine → esketamine

After the book: an anaesthetic becomes an antidepressant.

What happened?

New use · US 2019

The S form, as a nasal spray for treatment-resistant depression, given in clinics.

Back to Ayesha, Bilal and Sana

Rx Escitalopram 10 mg, once a day · cleared mainly by the liver enzyme CYP2C19

Ayesha

“I feel like myself again.”

No other medicines.

Explain it

Normal plughole

Nothing else changes her clearance, so the level settles inside the window after about a week (4–5 half-lives).

Bilal

“Far too strong.”

+ omeprazole for acidity

Explain it

Inhibitor: plughole narrowed

Omeprazole blocks CYP2C19, so clearance falls and escitalopram builds up (about 50% higher). Tell the doctor: lower the dose or change the acid tablet.

Sana

“Nothing has changed.”

+ carbamazepine for epilepsy

Explain it

Inducer: plughole widened

Carbamazepine makes the liver build extra enzymes, so escitalopram can be cleared before it reaches a working level. The doctor may raise the dose or choose another drug.

And always ask: is she taking it? Any new drugs, smoking changes, illness, older age? Next on the list, in Week 5: genes can narrow or widen the plughole too.

Chapter 3 · revision · pp. 79–100

Exam practice: getting in and spreading out

1Which best describes bioavailability?

  1. aHow long a drug stays in the body
  2. bThe proportion of a dose that enters the systemic circulation without being changed
  3. cThe apparent volume a drug spreads into
  4. dThe amount of blood the kidneys clean per hour

A fraction, and only the unchanged drug counts.

2A drug is 100% bioavailable injected but 40% swallowed. Why?

  1. aReceptors in the stomach hold on to it
  2. bPart is never absorbed, and part is broken down in the gut wall and liver before reaching the circulation
  3. cSwallowed drugs are excreted faster by the kidneys
  4. dThe blood–brain barrier blocks swallowed drugs

Incomplete absorption + first-pass metabolism.

3The time taken for the blood level to fall by half is the:

  1. aBioavailability
  2. bClearance
  3. cHalf-life
  4. dVolume of distribution

Half-life = 0.693 × Vd ÷ clearance.

4A drug's volume of distribution is 15,000 L. This tells you that:

  1. aIt dissolves in 15,000 L of body water
  2. bMost of it has left the blood for the tissues
  3. cIt is cleared from the body very fast
  4. dIts bioavailability is poor

Remember the detective: an apparent, not a real, volume.

Chapter 3 · revision · pp. 79–100

Exam practice: changing and leaving

5Which enzymes carry out most of the biotransformation of psychotropic drugs?

  1. aMonoamine oxidase in the brain
  2. bCytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver
  3. cEnzymes in saliva
  4. dAcetylcholinesterase in the blood

MAO breaks down transmitters, not most drugs.

6The main purpose of biotransformation is to:

  1. aSwitch drugs on so they can work
  2. bMake drugs more water-soluble so they can be excreted
  3. cHelp drugs cross the blood–brain barrier
  4. dStore drugs safely in body fat

Some products stay active, but that is not the purpose.

7A patient on lithium becomes dehydrated in a heatwave. The level rises because:

  1. aLiver enzymes are blocked
  2. bThe kidneys clear less lithium
  3. cIts bioavailability increases
  4. dIt binds less to proteins

Lithium is never metabolised: kidneys only.

8Which of these can raise the bioavailability of some swallowed drugs?

  1. aGrapefruit juice
  2. bA longer half-life
  3. cA larger volume of distribution
  4. dSmoking

It blocks CYP3A4 in the gut wall, so more gets through. Smoking does the opposite to some drugs (induces CYP1A2).

Five ideas to take away

1 The body decides how much drug reaches the receptor.

Bioavailability sets how much gets in; Vd, clearance and half-life set where it goes and how long it stays.

2 Fat-soluble gets in; biotransformation makes it water-soluble to get out.

The barrier from Lectures 1–2 explains both.

3 Half-life sets dosing and the time to steady state.

4–5 half-lives to build up, 4–5 to wash out.

4 Change the clearance, change the dose.

Other drugs, smoking, grapefruit, age and liver, kidney or heart disease all act like dose changes.

5 Blood levels guide a few drugs (lithium above all); kinetics matters most for predicting interactions.
